c: The + operator joins strings in order. For example, "CS" + "-" + "27" creates "CS-27", not a numerical total. The hyphen is one character.
OCR ERL uses zero-based indexing. text.substring(start, count) begins at start and takes count characters. text.left(n) takes the first n; text.right(n) takes the last n.
text.length counts all characters, including spaces and hyphens. text.upper and text.lower change the case of letters; neither changes digits. An extracted substring can also be converted.
For an identifier, select the required characters, change case, concatenate the parts and check the result. Validate input length before extracting characters that might not exist.

m.title: String manipulation · worked coding example
m.q: firstName = "Amelia" and team = "Falcons". Build the code AME-FAL and output its character count using OCR ERL.
st: The two variables store strings. The required identifier has two groups of three letters and a hyphen between them.
firstPart = firstName.left(3) gives "Ame"; secondPart = team.left(3) gives "Fal". The method left(3) takes exactly three characters.
code = firstPart.upper + "-" + secondPart.upper gives "AME-FAL". The + operator concatenates strings; the hyphen is text inside quotation marks.
print(code) produces AME-FAL. print(code.length) produces 7 because the code has 3 letters + 1 hyphen + 3 letters.

A school generates a pupil identifier from the FIRST three letters of firstName and the LAST three letters of surname, both uppercase, separated by a hyphen.

With firstName = "Georgia" and surname = "Mitchell", the required output is GEO-ELL.

Write an OCR Exam Reference Language algorithm that prints "Invalid" if EITHER name has fewer than three characters; otherwise print the identifier. [6 marks]

MODEL OCR ERL
firstName = "Georgia"
surname = "Mitchell"
if firstName.length >= 3 AND surname.length >= 3 then
    firstPart = firstName.left(3)
    lastPart = surname.right(3)
    print(firstPart.upper + "-" + lastPart.upper)
else
    print("Invalid")
endif

Expected output: GEO-ELL.
Marking: checks lengths of both inputs (2), correct left(3) (1), correct right(3) (1), uppercase and hyphen concatenation (1), correct valid/invalid output paths (1). Accept equivalent correct OCR ERL.

stretch.task: Adapt the worked example for student = "Harrison" and club = "Robotics": produce SON:ROB using right(3), left(3), .upper and a colon. Then print the length. Write OCR ERL.
stretch.hint: The last three letters of Harrison are son; the first three of Robotics are Rob. A colon counts as one character.
stretch.answer:
MODEL OCR ERL
student = "Harrison"
club = "Robotics"
a = student.right(3)
b = club.left(3)
code = a.upper + ":" + b.upper
print(code)
print(code.length)

Outputs: SON:ROB and 7.

mastery.task: Design an OCR ERL algorithm that accepts a surname and a two-character year code. If surname has fewer than three characters OR year code is not exactly two characters, print Invalid. Otherwise print the first three surname letters in uppercase, followed by a hyphen and the year code. Give one normal, one boundary and one invalid test.
mastery.hint: Check both lengths before calling .left(3). Use .length for each condition and concatenate strings with +.
mastery.answer:
MODEL OCR ERL
surname = input("Surname")
yearCode = input("Two-character year code")
if surname.length >= 3 AND yearCode.length == 2 then
    prefix = surname.left(3)
    print(prefix.upper + "-" + yearCode)
else
    print("Invalid")
endif

Tests: surname = "Mason", yearCode = "27" -> MAS-27 (normal); surname = "Lee", yearCode = "27" -> LEE-27 (boundary valid); surname = "Li", yearCode = "27" -> Invalid (invalid). Also test a one-character year code.

steps.title: 1 · Identify the input strings
steps.explanation: The program is combining parts of two strings, not adding numbers. The expected result contains six letters and one hyphen.

steps.title: 2 · Extract the characters
steps.explanation: left(3) takes the first three characters: Ame and Fal. Keep these as strings.

steps.title: 3 · Convert case and join
steps.explanation: The uppercase property changes the extracted text. The quoted hyphen contributes one character. Together these produce AME-FAL.

steps.title: 4 · Output and verify
steps.explanation: The first line prints AME-FAL. The second prints 7, because 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 characters.
steps.code:
firstName = "Amelia"
team = "Falcons"
firstPart = firstName.left(3)
secondPart = team.left(3)
code = firstPart.upper + "-" + secondPart.upper
print(code)
print(code.length)
